title: Right-tailed one-sample t-test for call handling time
scenario_markdown: A telecommunications customer support center deployed a new CRM ticketing interface. Operations management set a benchmark target mean resolution time of $\mu = 50.0\text{ seconds}$. Supervisors suspect that the new interface has increased handling times ($H_1: \mu > 50.0\text{ seconds}$). A random sample of $n = 20$ customer calls yields a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 53.1\text{ seconds}$ with sample standard deviation $s = 6.2\text{ seconds}$. Test the hypothesis at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$.
assumptions: Call handling times follow an approximately normal distribution
Independent random sample of support calls
Population standard deviation sigma is unknown and estimated by sample standard deviation s = 6.2 seconds, requiring Student's t distribution with df = n - 1 = 19

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: null_mu = 50.0, x_bar = 53.1, s = 6.2, n = 20. df = 19. SE = 6.2 / sqrt(20) = 1.38636. t = 3.1 / 1.38636 = 2.23607. One-tailed right tail p-value = 0.01878. Critical t_{0.05, 19} = 1.7291. Since p = 0.0188 < 0.05 and t = 2.236 > 1.729, reject H0. Excel: =T.DIST.RT(2.236, 19).

stages.prompt_markdown: Determine the appropriate degrees of freedom and compute the $t$ test statistic $t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}$.

options.hint_markdown: For a single sample t-test, degrees of freedom are $df = n - 1 = 20 - 1 = 19$.
Standard error divides $s$ by $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{20} \approx 4.472$, giving $1.386\text{ s}$.

stages.explanation_markdown: Because $\sigma$ is unknown, we use Student's $t$-distribution with $df = n - 1 = 20 - 1 = 19$. The standard error is $SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{6.2}{\sqrt{20}} = \frac{6.2}{4.472136} \approx 1.38636\text{ seconds}$. The test statistic is $t = \frac{53.1 - 50.0}{1.38636} = \frac{3.1}{1.38636} \approx +2.236$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate the right-tailed $p$-value and identify the corresponding Excel formula.

options.hint_markdown: The research hypothesis is strictly right-tailed ($H_1: \mu > 50$), so the p-value is the single upper tail area, not doubled.
In an upper-tailed test, the p-value is the area to the right of the test statistic ($1 - \text{CDF}$). Excel's `=T.DIST.RT` directly returns this right-tail probability.

stages.explanation_markdown: For an upper-tailed test ($H_1: \mu > 50.0$), the $p$-value is the area in the upper tail beyond $t = 2.236$ under a $t$-distribution with $19$ degrees of freedom: $P(T_{19} \ge 2.236) \approx 0.01878$ (or $1.88\%$). In Excel, `=T.DIST.RT(2.236, 19)` yields $0.0188$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Comparing the test statistic and $p$-value to $\alpha = 0.05$ (critical value $t_{0.05, 19} = 1.729$), what is the operational conclusion?

options.text_markdown: Reject $H_0$ because $p\text{-value} = 0.0188 < 0.05$ (and $t = 2.236 > 1.729$). There is statistically significant evidence that the new interface has increased mean handling time.
Fail to reject $H_0$ because a sample of $n = 20$ is too small to make any valid statistical conclusion.
options.hint_markdown: Student's t distribution explicitly accounts for smaller sample sizes through degrees of freedom; with p < 0.05, rejection is fully justified.

options.text_markdown: Fail to reject $H_0$ because $t = 2.236$ does not exceed $Z^* = 2.576$.
options.hint_markdown: The test uses alpha = 0.05 with df = 19, where critical cutoff is t = 1.729, not 2.576.

stages.explanation_markdown: Because the $p$-value ($0.0188$) is less than $\alpha = 0.05$ (and the test statistic $t = 2.236$ exceeds the critical threshold $t_{0.05, 19} = 1.729$), we reject $H_0$. Operations management has statistically significant evidence that the new CRM interface has prolonged call handling times beyond the $50\text{ second}$ target.
